title: The Lindy Effect on startup potential: 2x is assumed, 10x must be proven
summary: Jason Cohen applies the Lindy Effect to startup growth: however big you are, you can probably double by doing what you already do, but 10x needs new channels, innovation, or hyper-growth. He explains why early tactics don't scale and why investors fixate on fast growth.

principles.text: You can probably double by repeating what works, but 10x requires innovation.
principles.quote: You can probably double your size by doing what you're already doing, but 10x will require innovation.

principles.text: Early-customer tactics rarely scale: what got you 10 customers won't get you 100.
principles.quote: the actions that got you your first 10 customers are probably not sufficient for generating 100, even though they're probably sufficient for getting another 10.

principles.text: A single marketing channel has limited inventory, so 10x needs multiple new channels.
principles.quote: it's unlikely that there is 10x the inventory inside that one channel to get you to 10,000 customers. Thus you'll need to make other channels work

principles.text: Very fast growth at meaningful size is the proof that 10x is within reach.
principles.quote: One answer is having very fast growth. If you're doubling every six months, you clearly have line-of-sight for more growth than just 2x.

principles.text: Investors and founders chasing huge outcomes obsess over hyper-growth because it's the only route to something enormous.
principles.quote: This is why investors (and founders) wishing to build enormous companies are so fixated on hyper-growth. It's the only way to have even the potential of building something enormous.

principles.text: Break the Lindy Effect by expanding into an adjacency: keep one foot in your strength, step into something riskier with bigger upside.
principles.quote: Another way to break the Lindy Effect is to change something substantial. I think of this as expanding into an adjacency.
